tag: Regulation is a rule or order issued by a government agency, often with the force of law (narrow, agency-rule reading); federal regulations appear in the Federal Register and CFR
source: Merriam-Webster Legal Dictionary
title: Legal Definition of REGULATION
context: Legal Definition, noun, sense 2 with usage note
quote: 2: an authoritative rule specifically: a rule or order issued by a government agency and often having the force of law see also Administrative Procedure Act Note: An agency is often delegated the power to issue regulations by the legislation that created it. Regulations must be made in accordance with prescribed procedures, such as those set out in the federal or a state Administrative Procedure Act. Federal regulations are first published in the Federal Register and later codified in the Code of Federal Regulations.

tag: Regulation has two ordinary senses: any authoritative rule on details or procedure, or a rule issued by a government agency with the force of law
source: Merriam-Webster Dictionary
title: Regulation Definition & Meaning
quote: 2 a: an authoritative rule dealing with details or procedure safety regulations b: a rule or order issued by an executive authority or regulatory agency of a government and having the force of law

tag: Regulation is a principle, rule, or law designed to control or govern conduct, or a governmental order with the force of law
source: American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 5th ed.
author: HarperCollins Publishers
title: regulation
quote: 2. A principle, rule, or law designed to control or govern conduct. 3. A governmental order having the force of law.

tag: Regulation is the act of regulating, or a rule or order prescribed for management or government; a regulating principle; a precept
source: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed.) via The Law Dictionary
title: REGULATION
quote: The act of regulating; a rule or order prescribed for management or government; a regulating principle; a precept.

tag: A regulation is a law, rule, or order prescribed by any authority (not only agencies), especially to regulate conduct
source: Dictionary.com
title: REGULATION Definition & Meaning
quote: a law, rule, or other order prescribed by authority, especially to regulate conduct.

tag: A regulation is a rule made and maintained by an authority, typically a governmental agency, to control or govern conduct within its jurisdiction; agencies are delegated legislative power to create them
source: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Wex Legal Dictionary
author: Wex Definitions Team
title: regulation
quote: A regulation is a rule made and maintained by an authority, typically a governmental agency, to control or govern conduct within its jurisdiction. Governmental administrative agencies have specific authority to regulate conduct within their areas of responsibility. These agencies are delegated legislative power to create and enforce rules, known as "regulations."

tag: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, a "rule" is any agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy
source: 5 U.S.C. 551(4) (Administrative Procedure Act), Cornell LII
author: U.S. Congress
title: 5 U.S. Code Sec. 551 - Definitions
quote: (4) "rule" means the whole or a part of an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or describing the organization, procedure, or practice requirements of an agency and includes the approval or prescription for the future of rates, wages, corporate or financial structures or reorganizations thereof, prices, facilities, appliances, services or allowances therefor or of valuations, costs, or accounting, or practices bearing on any of the foregoing;

tag: Executive Order 12866 defines "regulation" as an agency statement the agency intends to have the force and effect of law, with listed exclusions (formal rulemaking, military/foreign affairs, internal management)
source: Executive Order 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review (American Presidency Project)
author: President William J. Clinton
title: Executive Order 12866 - Regulatory Planning and Review
quote: (d) "Regulation" or "rule" means an agency statement of general applicability and future effect, which the agency intends to have the force and effect of law, that is designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or to describe the procedure or practice requirements of an agency. It does not, however, include: (1) Regulations or rules issued in accordance with the formal rulemaking provisions of 5 U.S.C. 556, 557; (2) Regulations or rules that pertain to a military or foreign affairs function of the United States, other than procurement regulations and regulations involving the import or export of non-defense articles and services; (3) Regulations or rules that are limited to agency organization, management, or personnel matters; or (4) Any other category of regulations exempted by the Administrator of OIRA.

tag: Regulation is one of government's basic tools to implement public policy; regulations generally start with an act of Congress, and "rule" and "regulation" are often used interchangeably
source: Congressional Research Service (via EveryCRSReport.com)
author: Curtis W. Copeland
title: The Federal Rulemaking Process: An Overview (RL32240)
quote: Federal regulation, like taxing and spending, is one of the basic tools of government used to implement public policy. Although not as frequently examined as congressional or presidential policy making, the process of developing and framing rules is viewed by some as central to the definition and implementation of public policy in the United States. Regulations generally start with an act of Congress, and are the means by which statutes are implemented and specific requirements are established. The terms "rule" or "regulation" are often used interchangeably in discussions of the federal regulatory process. The Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 defines a rule as "the whole or part of an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy."

tag: EPA: regulations are mandatory requirements, written under congressional authorization to implement laws, that can apply to individuals, businesses, governments, and others
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
author: EPA
title: Regulations
quote: EPA is called a regulatory agency because Congress authorizes us to write regulations that explain the technical, operational, and legal details necessary to implement laws. Regulations are mandatory requirements that can apply to individuals, businesses, state or local governments, non-profit institutions, or others.

tag: Broad reading: regulation is government intervention in the private domain, or the binding legal rule implementing it, created by any legislative, executive, administrative, or judicial body
source: Yale Journal on Regulation (Bulletin)
author: Barak Orbach
title: What is Regulation?
quote: So what does regulation mean? We return to the starting point-the intuitive understanding of the word "regulation": government intervention in the private domain or a legal rule that implements such intervention. The implementing rule is a binding legal norm created by a state organ that intends to shape the conduct of individuals and firms. The state organ, the regulator, may be any legislative, executive, administrative, or judicial body that has the legal power to create a binding legal norm. This general definition is broader than "restrictions," "rules promulgated by administrative agencies," "laws that serve interest groups," and related common perceptions of the word "regulation."

tag: Economists disagree on what regulation is - from price/entry controls in utilities to every policy altering market outcomes; Noll argues it fits the middle level: administrative processes controlling private market interactions
source: Caltech Social Science Working Paper 324 (Hoover Institution conference)
author: Roger G. Noll
title: What is Regulation?
quote: The economics literature contains no consistent, generally accepted definition of regulation. Some standard references define regulation as the control of prices, profits and entry in the utility sector, while others include in the definition literally every public policy that alters market outcomes, including tariffs, commodity-specific taxes, and import quotas. This paper argues that definitions should have a basis in theory, and that regulatory research suggests three levels of generality of public policy that correspond to coherent theoretical analysis: the previous two, plus an intermediate level that covers the use of administrative processes to control private market interactions. Regulation is argued to be most appropriately applied to this intermediate level, and examples are given to justify the usefulness of the proposed classification scheme.

tag: Command-and-control regulation = uniform technology- or performance-based standards that leave little flexibility in how firms comply
source: Resources for the Future Discussion Paper 01-53
author: Robert N. Stavins
title: Lessons From the American Experiment With Market-Based Environmental Policies
quote: By way of contrast, conventional approaches to regulating the environment are often referred to as "command-and-control" regulations, since they allow relatively little flexibility in the means of achieving goals. Such regulations tend to force firms to take on similar shares of the pollution-control burden, regardless of the cost. Command-and-control regulations do this by setting uniform standards for firms, the most prevalent of which are technology- and performance-based standards. Technology-based standards specify the method, and sometimes the actual equipment, that firms must use to comply with a particular regulation. A performance standard sets a uniform control target for firms, while allowing some latitude in how this target is met.

tag: Regulation includes market-based instruments (tradable permits, pollution charges) that steer behavior through market signals rather than explicit directives - regulation need not be command-and-control
source: Resources for the Future Discussion Paper 01-53
author: Robert N. Stavins
title: Lessons From the American Experiment With Market-Based Environmental Policies
quote: Market-based instruments are regulations that encourage behavior through market signals rather than through explicit directives regarding pollution control levels or methods.

tag: To regulate means to govern by rule, bring under the control of law or authority, or make regulations for or concerning something
source: Merriam-Webster Dictionary
title: REGULATE Definition & Meaning
quote: 1 a: to govern or direct according to rule b (1): to bring under the control of law or constituted authority (2): to make regulations for or concerning regulate the industries of a country

tag: To regulate means to control or direct according to rule, principle, or law, or to adjust to a specification
source: American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 5th ed.
author: HarperCollins Publishers
title: regulate
quote: 1. To control or direct according to rule, principle, or law. 2. To adjust to a particular specification or requirement: regulate temperature. 3. To adjust (a mechanism) for accurate and proper functioning. 4. To put or maintain in order: regulate one's eating habits.

tag: 1828 Webster: to regulate is to adjust by rule or method, to put in good order, or to subject to rules or restrictions (e.g., to regulate trade)
source: Webster's Dictionary 1828 (American Dictionary of the English Language)
author: Noah Webster
title: Regulate - Webster's Dictionary 1828
quote: 1. To adjust by rule, method or established mode; as, to regulate weights and measures; to regulate the assize of bread; to regulate our moral conduct by the laws of God and of society; to regulate our manners by the customary forms. 2. To put in good order; as, to regulate the disordered state of a nation or its finances. 3. To subject to rules or restrictions; as, to regulate trade; to regulate diet.

tag: Black's (2nd ed.): the power to regulate is the power to prescribe the rules by which something is governed, and includes control of all its instrumentalities
source: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed.) via The Law Dictionary
title: REGULATE
context: Black's Law Dictionary, 2nd Ed., citing Gloucester Ferry Co. v. Pennsylvania
quote: The power to regulate commerce, vested in congress, is the power to prescribe the rules by which it shall be governed, that is, the conditions upon which it shall be conducted, to determine when it shall be free, and when subject to duties or other exactions. The power also embraces within its control all the instrumentalities by which that commerce may be carried on, and the means by which it may be aided and encouraged.

tag: Chief Justice Marshall: to regulate means "to prescribe the rule by which commerce is to be governed" - a complete power limited only by the Constitution
source: Gibbons v. Ogden, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 1 (1824) (Cornell LII)
author: Chief Justice John Marshall
title: GIBBONS, Appellant, v. OGDEN, Respondent.
context: Opinion of the Court, 22 U.S. at 196
quote: It is the power to regulate; that is, to prescribe the rule by which commerce is to be governed. This power, like all others vested in Congress, is complete in itself, may be exercised to its utmost extent, and acknowledges no limitations, other than are prescribed in the constitution.

tag: CRS Constitution Annotated: the Court reads "regulate" as the power to prescribe conditions and rules, keep channels open, and regulate prices and terms
source: Constitution Annotated (Congressional Research Service) via Cornell LII
author: Congressional Research Service
title: Meaning of Regulate in the Commerce Clause (ArtI.S8.C3.4)
quote: The Court has interpreted "regulate" in the Commerce Clause as Congress's power to prescribe conditions and rules for commercial transactions, keep channels of commerce open, and regulate prices and terms of sale.

tag: Narrow reading: "to regulate" far more commonly meant "to adjust by rule or method," which presupposes something already there to adjust
source: National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, 567 U.S. 519 (2012) (Cornell LII)
author: Chief Justice John Roberts (n.4)
title: NATIONAL FEDERATION OF INDEPENDENT BUSINESS v. SEBELIUS
quote: It is unlikely that the Framers had such an obscure meaning in mind when they used the word "regulate." Far more commonly, "[t]o regulate" meant "[t]o adjust by rule or method," which presupposes something to adjust.

tag: Broad reading: at the time of the Constitution, "to regulate" meant, among other things, "to require action" (D.C. Circuit, quoted by Ginsburg)
source: National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, 567 U.S. 519 (2012) (Cornell LII)
author: Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg
title: NATIONAL FEDERATION OF INDEPENDENT BUSINESS v. SEBELIUS
context: Opinion of Ginsburg, J., concurring in part, concurring in the judgment in part, and dissenting in part
quote: Indeed, as the D. C. Circuit observed, "[a]t the time the Constitution was [framed], to 'regulate' meant," among other things, "to require action." See Seven-Sky v. Holder, 661 F. 3d 1, 16 (2011).

tag: "For" indicates purpose, an intended goal, or the object of an activity (the policy is aimed at / designed for the purpose of regulation)
source: Merriam-Webster Dictionary
title: FOR Definition & Meaning
quote: 1 a -used as a function word to indicate purpose a grant for studying medicine b -used as a function word to indicate an intended goal left for home acted for the best c -used as a function word to indicate the object or recipient of a perception, desire, or activity now for a good rest run for your life an eye for a bargain

tag: "For" can mean "with respect to; concerning" (policy for regulation = policy concerning / about regulation)
source: Merriam-Webster Dictionary
title: FOR Definition & Meaning
quote: 7: with respect to: concerning a stickler for detail heavy for its size

tag: "For" indicates the object, aim, or purpose of an action or activity
source: American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 5th ed.
author: HarperCollins Publishers
title: for
quote: 1. a. Used to indicate the object, aim, or purpose of an action or activity: trained for the ministry; put the house up for sale; plans to run for senator. b. Used to indicate a destination: headed off for town.

tag: "For" can mean "as regards; concerning"
source: American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, 5th ed.
author: HarperCollins Publishers
title: for
quote: 10. a. As regards; concerning: a stickler for neatness. b. Considering the nature or usual character of: was spry for his advanced age. c. In honor of: named for her grandmother.

tag: "For" can mean "intended to be given to" (recipient sense, e.g., a message for you)
source: Cambridge Dictionary
title: FOR | English meaning
quote: intended to be given to: There's a phone message for you. I'd better buy something for the new baby. There's a prize for the fastest three runners in each category.

tag: "Regulation of" something means the act of controlling that thing
source: Cambridge Dictionary
title: REGULATION | English meaning
quote: [U] the act of controlling something: regulation of They are demanding tighter regulation of the marketing of alcohol to teenagers. The thermostat allows regulation of the temperature to a fine degree. Regulation of your emotions is important in a business context.

tag: Clean Water Act: requires the regulation of point sources (stationary discharge locations); discharging from a point source without an NPDES permit is illegal
source: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Wex Legal Dictionary
title: Clean Water Act (CWA)
quote: In addition to monitoring water quality standards, the CWA requires the regulation of point sources, or stationary locations that discharge pollution into water. Under CWA §301, discharge of a pollutant from a point source into waters of the United States is illegal without a National Pollution Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permit.

tag: Constitutional use of "rules for the ... regulation of": Congress is empowered to make rules governing a subject
source: U.S. Constitution, Article I (Cornell LII)
author: Framers
title: Article I | U.S. Constitution
quote: To make rules for the government and regulation of the land and naval forces;

tag: Narrow reading: the power of "regulation of" a subject presupposes the subject already exists - it does not include bringing the regulated thing into existence
source: National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, 567 U.S. 519 (2012) (Cornell LII)
author: Chief Justice John Roberts
title: NATIONAL FEDERATION OF INDEPENDENT BUSINESS v. SEBELIUS
context: Opinion of Roberts, C.J., Part III-A
quote: If the power to regulate the armed forces or the value of money included the power to bring the subject of the regulation into existence, the specific grant of such powers would have been unnecessary. The language of the Constitution reflects the natural understanding that the power to regulate assumes there is already something to be regulated.

tag: Clean Water Act context: "regulation of water pollution" was left almost entirely to the States for most of U.S. history (common-law nuisance suits, then state regulatory agencies)
source: Sackett v. EPA, 598 U.S. 651 (2023) (Cornell LII)
author: Justice Samuel Alito
title: SACKETT v. EPA
context: Opinion of the Court, Part I-A
quote: For most of this Nation's history, the regulation of water pollution was left almost entirely to the States and their subdivisions. The common law permitted aggrieved parties to bring nuisance suits against polluters. But as industrial production and population growth increased the quantity and toxicity of pollution, States gradually shifted to enforcement by regulatory agencies.

tag: Regulation of X can include forbidding and punishing conduct, not just conditioning it - the Court treats prohibition as a form of regulation (police-power style)
source: Constitution Annotated (Congressional Research Service) via Cornell LII, quoting Brooks v. United States, 267 U.S. 432 (1925)
author: Congressional Research Service
title: Meaning of Regulate in the Commerce Clause (ArtI.S8.C3.4)
quote: Congress can certainly regulate interstate commerce to the extent of forbidding and punishing the use of such commerce as an agency to promote immorality, dishonesty, or the spread of any evil or harm to the people of other states from the state of origin. In doing this, it is merely exercising the police power, for the benefit of the public, within the field of interstate commerce.
